title: Loops and Iteration Tools
subtitle: Phase 1 - Python Foundations
tagline: Loops are for algorithms; vectorisation is for data. Learn loops properly to know when to leave them.
prerequisites: Comfort with the earlier topics of Data Science + Python Foundations.
Python installed and a working notebook environment (see Days 4-5).
learning_objectives: Write for and while loops with correct termination conditions.
Use range, enumerate and zip to avoid index bookkeeping bugs.
Control loops with break, continue and the often-forgotten for/else.
Recognise when a loop over rows is the wrong tool.
Bound nested-loop complexity and choose the right data structure to fix it.
why_this_matters: Loops are how you write algorithms - and also how you accidentally write an O(n^2) pipeline over a million rows. Learning them well includes learning when to hand the work to NumPy or pandas instead.

concept.what: A for loop iterates over any iterable (list, tuple, dict, string, file, generator, DataFrame column). A while loop repeats while a condition holds and must be made to terminate. Both support break (exit now), continue (skip to next iteration) and an else clause that runs only if the loop finished without break.
concept.why: Grouping, filtering and accumulating are loops underneath. Writing them explicitly teaches the mechanics; recognising the vectorised equivalent is what makes code fast enough for real data.
concept.how: Prefer `for item in iterable` over index arithmetic; add enumerate() when you need the index, zip() to walk two sequences together, and items() for dictionaries. Use while for unknown-iteration problems (convergence, retry, queue drain) with an explicit guard to avoid infinite loops.
concept.intuition: A loop is a conveyor belt: the body does one operation per item. The cost of the whole belt is (work per item) x (number of items), so improving either factor improves everything.
concept.analogy: Tuning a radio: a for loop scans a known list of stations; a while loop keeps turning until the signal matches (unknown number of turns) - and you need a maximum-turn guard so you do not burn out the dial.
concept.internals: for loop calls iter(obj) then next() until StopIteration. Each iteration in CPython is interpreted bytecode, which is why a Python-level loop costs roughly 50-100 ns per simple iteration while a NumPy array operation runs in compiled C over contiguous memory - often 20-100x faster.
concept.deep: Nested loops multiply: two loops over 10^4 items is 10^8 operations. The fix is structural, not stylistic - build a dict/set for lookup (Day 9), sort-and-sweep, or vectorise. Also note loop-carried dependencies prevent vectorisation; if each step needs the previous result, you must loop (or use cumulative functions like np.cumsum).
concept.math: Total work = iterations x cost per iteration. Estimating this before writing code is a professional habit: 1e6 rows x 1e3 comparisons is a thousand million operations, which no amount of syntax sugar fixes - only a boundary change (hash lookup, vectorisation, database index) will.

visual.title: Loop cost = items x per-item work
visual.caption: Improving either factor improves throughput: reduce per-item work (vectorise, avoid lookups) or reduce items (filter early, sample, aggregate at source).

code_examples.title: The four idioms that replace index bookkeeping
code_examples.label: SOURCE
code_examples.code:
sales = [220, 340, 180, 500]

# 1. Direct iteration (never use range(len(x)) unless you truly need the index)
total = 0
for amount in sales:
    total += amount
print("total:", total)

# 2. enumerate when you need position + value
for i, amount in enumerate(sales, start=1):
    print(f"row {i}: {amount}")

# 3. zip to walk two sequences together (stops at the shortest)
targets = [200, 300, 200, 450]
for amount, target in zip(sales, targets):
    status = "hit" if amount >= target else "miss"
    print(f"{amount} vs {target}: {status}")

# 4. dict iteration with .items()
regions = {"north": 120, "south": 90}
for name, amount in regions.items():
    print(name, amount)

# Accumulating into a dict (the most common analytics loop)
by_parity = {"even": 0, "odd": 0}
for amount in sales:
    by_parity["even" if amount % 2 == 0 else "odd"] += amount
print(by_parity)

# The vectorised equivalent - learn to see this
import numpy as np
arr = np.array(sales)
print("numpy sum:", arr.sum(), "| mean:", arr.mean(), "| >=200:", (arr >= 200).sum())

line_by_line: Line 4-6: iterating the values directly is the clearest form; no indexes to get wrong.
Line 9-10: enumerate gives a counter; start=1 is handy for human-readable output (Excel-like row numbers).
Line 13-16: zip pairs two sequences; if lengths differ it silently stops at the shortest, so assert lengths first.
Line 19-20: iterating .items() yields (key, value) pairs - the standard pattern for configuration and lookups.
Line 23-25: building aggregates in a loop is the core of grouping; note how quickly this becomes a groupby in pandas (Day 62).
Line 28-29: the vectorised equivalents express the same intent without a loop - the mindset shift that Phase 3 formalises.

code_examples.title: while loops, loop control, and the for/else that surprises everyone
code_examples.label: EXPLANATION
code_examples.output:
doubled after 15 years -> 2078.93
processing 4
found at index 1
no negatives found
attempt 1 ok=False
attempt 2 ok=True
pairs checked: 1225  (naive would be 2500)
line_by_line: Line 4-7: while with a compound condition includes a safety bound (years < 40) so a logic error cannot hang the process.
Line 10-16: continue skips the rest of the iteration; break exits the loop entirely. Order matters: check skip conditions before early exits.
Line 19-27: for/else separates 'found' from 'exhausted'. It is clearer than a found flag and shows up in binary search and validation code.
Line 30-38: the retry-with-limit pattern is exactly how production API calls are written (Day 27). The else clause is the alert path.
Line 41-46: nested loops can be pruned with early exits, but the structural fix for big data is a hash lookup or vectorisation - not more breaks.

common_mistakes.why: It adds index arithmetic, hurts readability and invites off-by-one errors.
common_mistakes.fix: Iterate directly; add enumerate() when you need the index.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing a while loop without a guaranteed exit.
common_mistakes.why: A logic error hangs the process (or the notebook kernel) and burns time.
common_mistakes.fix: Always include a bound (`while cond and attempts < MAX`) and log the iterations.

common_mistakes.mistake: Modifying a list while iterating over it.
common_mistakes.why: Indexes shift, so elements are skipped silently.
common_mistakes.fix: Iterate over a copy or build a new list with a comprehension.

common_mistakes.mistake: Looping over DataFrame rows with iterrows() for aggregation.
common_mistakes.why: It is 100-1000x slower than the vectorised equivalent and loses dtypes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use groupby/vectorised operations; if you must loop, use itertuples() and only on small slices.

debugging.symptom: The loop runs forever with no output.
debugging.cause: The condition never becomes false (missing increment, or comparing incompatible types).
debugging.fix: Add a counter and print it every N iterations; add a hard iteration cap while debugging.

debugging.symptom: Results are correct but the script takes hours.
debugging.cause: Nested loop with a membership test (O(n^2)).
debugging.fix: Build a set/dict for O(1) lookups; measure before and after with time.perf_counter.

debugging.symptom: for/else prints 'not found' even though it was found.
debugging.cause: Using `return` or a flag inside the loop instead of break, so else still runs.
debugging.fix: Use break for the found case; the else clause triggers only on exhaustion.

practice.task: Sum all even numbers between 1 and 100 using a loop, then verify with sum(range(2, 101, 2)).
practice.hint: Accumulator plus a condition, or a step in range.

practice.task: Given two lists of customer ids, print the ids present in both using ONE loop and set membership.
practice.hint: Build a set from one list, then loop the other.
practice.solution: O(n) instead of O(n^2) - the standard interview framing.

practice.task: Implement a retry loop that calls a function returning random success/failure, retries up to 5 times with increasing sleep, and raises a clear error if all attempts fail.
practice.solution: Prints attempts, sleeps between them, raises RuntimeError with the last error.

mini_challenge.title: Loop versus vector: measured
mini_challenge.brief: Compute the mean, median and count above threshold for 1e6 random numbers twice: once with a Python loop and once with NumPy. Report both timings and the speed-up.
mini_challenge.deliverable: A notebook cell with both implementations, timings, and identical results asserted.
mini_challenge.stretch: Extend to grouping by a category column and compare with pandas groupby.

interview_questions.q: When would you use a while loop instead of a for loop?
interview_questions.a: When the number of iterations is unknown: convergence, retry with backoff, draining a queue, reading a stream. Always add an upper bound so a logic error cannot hang the process.

interview_questions.q: What does the else clause on a for loop do?
interview_questions.a: It runs only if the loop completed without break - the idiom for 'not found' branches in search algorithms.

interview_questions.q: How do you speed up a nested loop in a data pipeline?
interview_questions.a: First remove the quadratic behaviour: build a dict/set for O(1) lookups, or join in SQL/pandas. Then vectorise with NumPy/pandas if the operation is elementwise. Measure both versions to prove the gain.

interview_questions.q: Why is iterating pandas rows considered bad practice?
interview_questions.a: iterrows boxes each value into Python objects and rebuilds a Series per row, losing dtype efficiency; it is 100-1000x slower than vectorised ops. Use itertuples or, better, a vectorised/grouped formulation.

real_world: Batch jobs that 'work on the sample, fail on production' are usually loops whose per-iteration cost was fine for 1,000 rows and fatal for 50 million. Estimating work before coding is a senior habit you can start today.
production: Always bound loops in production code (max iterations, timeouts) and log progress for long jobs.
Prefer chunked processing with progress logging over one giant loop that gives no feedback.
If a job takes longer than expected, profile before optimising syntax: the problem is usually algorithmic.
recap: Iterate iterables directly; use enumerate and zip to avoid index bookkeeping.
while loops need an explicit termination guard.
break exits, continue skips, for/else handles the exhausted case.
Loop cost = items x per-item work; fix the bigger factor first.
Avoid row-wise loops on DataFrames - vectorise or group instead.

quiz.q: Which loop form gives both index and value?
quiz.explain: enumerate yields (index, value) pairs; you can set start=1 for human numbering.

quiz.q: When does a for loop's else block execute?
options: When the loop finishes without hitting break
Only when the loop body raises
quiz.explain: It is the 'not found' branch in search loops.

quiz.q: What is the complexity problem with `for a in list_a: if a in list_b:` for large lists?
options: It is O(n*m) - use a set for O(n+m)
It is fine because Python is fast
quiz.explain: Membership on a list is O(n); with a set it becomes O(1) per lookup.

quiz.q: `zip(a, b)` with len(a)=5 and len(b)=3 yields:
options: 3 pairs - it stops at the shortest
quiz.explain: Zip truncates silently; assert equal lengths when that would be a data error.

quiz.q: Which is the production-safe retry pattern?
options: while attempts < MAX with backoff and an alert on exhaustion
Recursive retry without a base case
quiz.explain: Bounded retries with backoff prevent infinite loops and thundering-herd behaviour.

flashcards.back: Index plus value without index bookkeeping.
Walk two sequences together; truncates to the shortest.
Executes only when no break occurred.
Always include a maximum iteration guard.
items x per-item work - optimise the dominant factor.
NumPy/pandas replace row loops at 20-100x speed.
